General Polygon Construction

InductionAlgorithmsLogic
Game: Build a hidden polygon from a set of centres and turning angles.
How to play: Drag a centre to move it, or change its angle in the boxes. The polygon appears when the angles allow it.
Look for the math

Three centrest of squares on a triangle determine the triangle. The same trick works for any number of points and angles.

Spin the point around

At each centre Mi, rotate a point by the angle ai. Doing this for all centres composes into a single rotation by the total angle. If the total is not a multiple of 360°, that rotation has one fixed point — and it is the first vertex A1 of the hidden polygon. Rotate A1 by each angle in turn to find the other vertices.

Why the triangles fit

Each rotation about Mi sends Ai to Ai+1, so those two points are the same distance from Mi and the angle between them is exactly ai: the triangle is isosceles as required. The logic test checks this on hundreds of random centre sets and angle triples, and covers the page's 60°, 90° and 180° examples.

When it breaks

If the angles add to a multiple of 360°, the composite rotation is a translation or the identity: there is no single fixed point, so the construction has no unique answer. The page asks why; the fixed-point equation (I − R)F = t has no solution because I − R is singular exactly in that case.

Set all three angles to 90° (the squares problem), then set them to 60° (equilateral triangles). What changes?
